title: The life cycle of a star

notes.definition: A star goes through a life cycle from a nebula to its final state; the stages after the main sequence depend on the size (mass) of the star. Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements, and supernovae spread them through the universe.
explanation: All stars begin as a nebula, a cloud of dust and gas (mostly hydrogen). Gravity pulls the material together. As it collapses it becomes denser and hotter, forming a protostar. When the core becomes hot and dense enough, hydrogen nuclei start to fuse into helium nuclei, releasing energy. The star is now a main sequence star. It is stable because the outward pressure from fusion energy balances the inward pull of gravity. Stars spend most of their lives in this stage.

When a star about the same size as the Sun runs low on hydrogen in its core, it expands to become a red giant. In a red giant, helium nuclei fuse to form heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen. Eventually fusion stops, and the outer layers drift away. The hot, dense core that remains collapses to become a white dwarf, which is very small and very hot. As it cools, it fades and becomes a black dwarf, which no longer emits significant energy.

A star much more massive than the Sun follows a different path. After the main sequence, it expands to become a red super giant. Fusion continues, producing heavier and heavier elements, up to iron. When fusion can go no further, the core collapses suddenly and the star explodes in a supernova, which can briefly outshine a whole galaxy. What remains of the core forms either a neutron star (an extremely dense object made of neutrons) or, if the star was massive enough, a black hole, whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements. Hydrogen fuses to helium in main sequence stars. In red giants and red super giants, helium and then heavier nuclei fuse to make elements up to iron. Elements heavier than iron, such as gold and uranium, are produced only in a supernova, where enormous amounts of energy are available. The explosion of a massive star distributes all of these elements throughout the universe.

Material thrown out by supernovae mixes with gas in space and forms new nebulae, from which new stars and planets form. This is why the Earth, and our own bodies, contain elements such as carbon, oxygen, iron and gold: these elements were made inside stars that existed before the Sun.
keyFacts: Nebula → protostar → main sequence star for all stars.
In a main sequence star, gravity inwards balances outward pressure from fusion.
Sun-sized star: main sequence → red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf.
Massive star: main sequence → red super giant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.
The life cycle a star follows is determined by its size (mass).
Main sequence: hydrogen fuses to form helium.
Red giants and super giants fuse helium and heavier nuclei, up to iron.
Elements heavier than iron are made in a supernova.
Supernovae distribute elements throughout the universe.
Fusion in stars produces all naturally occurring elements.

keyTerms.definition: A hot, dense ball of gas forming from a collapsing nebula, before fusion has started.
A stable star fusing hydrogen into helium, with gravity and fusion pressure balanced.
A large, cooler star that a Sun-sized star becomes after the main sequence.
The small, hot, dense core left behind by a red giant.
A white dwarf that has cooled so that it no longer emits significant energy.
A very large star formed from a star much more massive than the Sun after the main sequence.
The explosion of a red super giant, in which elements heavier than iron are made.
An extremely dense remnant of a supernova, made mostly of neutrons.
A remnant of a very massive star with gravity so strong that not even light can escape.

workedExamples.title: Ordering the stages
workedExamples.question: Put these stages for a star like the Sun in order: white dwarf, nebula, red giant, main sequence, protostar, black dwarf.
steps: All stars start as a nebula, then a protostar, then a main sequence star.
A Sun-sized star then becomes a red giant.
It leaves a white dwarf which cools to a black dwarf.
workedExamples.answer: Nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf.

workedExamples.title: Where elements come from
workedExamples.question: A gold ring contains gold atoms. Explain where these atoms were made.
steps: Elements heavier than iron are only made in a supernova.
The supernova spread the gold into space, where it became part of the nebula that formed the solar system and the Earth.
workedExamples.answer: In a supernova explosion of a massive star, which spread them into the material that formed the Earth.

diagrams.title: Life cycle of a star
diagrams.caption: Every star starts as a nebula, becomes a protostar, then a main sequence star. A star about the size of the Sun becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf and finally a black dwarf. A much more massive star becomes a red super giant, explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star or a black hole.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all stars end as black holes.
misconceptions.right: In fact only the most massive stars become black holes; Sun-sized stars become white dwarfs then black dwarfs, and some massive stars leave neutron stars.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the Sun will explode as a supernova.
misconceptions.right: In fact the Sun is not massive enough; it will become a red giant, then a white dwarf.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all elements were made in the Big Bang.
misconceptions.right: In fact the Big Bang made mainly hydrogen and helium; heavier elements were made by fusion in stars, and those heavier than iron in supernovae.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse a red giant with a red super giant.
misconceptions.right: In fact a red giant comes from a Sun-sized star; a red super giant comes from a much more massive star and ends in a supernova.

realWorld: Astronomers observed supernova SN 1987A in a nearby galaxy, confirming predictions about massive star deaths.
The gold, iron and carbon on Earth were made inside stars that died before the Sun was born.
Pulsars, rapidly spinning neutron stars, were discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell in 1967.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only, not Combined Science.
Describe the life cycle of a star the size of the Sun and of a star much more massive than the Sun.
Explain how fusion processes lead to the formation of new elements, including elements heavier than iron in supernovae.
examTips: Learn both paths as a flowchart; the shared start is nebula, protostar, main sequence.
Spell the stages exactly as AQA does: 'red super giant', 'white dwarf', 'black dwarf', 'neutron star'.
If asked which path a star takes, say it depends on the size (mass) of the star.
For element formation, state that elements up to iron form by fusion in stars and elements heavier than iron form in a supernova.
summary: All stars: nebula, protostar, main sequence.
Sun-sized: red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf.
Massive: red super giant, supernova, neutron star or black hole.
Fusion in stars makes elements up to iron.
Elements heavier than iron are made in supernovae.
Supernovae spread elements through the universe.

flashcards.front: What does every star begin as?
flashcards.back: A nebula (cloud of dust and gas).

flashcards.front: What forms when gravity pulls a nebula together?
What happens in a main sequence star?
flashcards.back: Hydrogen fuses into helium; gravity and fusion pressure are balanced.

flashcards.front: Life cycle of a Sun-sized star after the main sequence
flashcards.back: Red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf.

flashcards.front: Life cycle of a massive star after the main sequence
flashcards.back: Red super giant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

flashcards.front: What decides which life cycle a star follows?

flashcards.back: The explosion of a red super giant (a massive star).

flashcards.front: Where are elements heavier than iron made?
How are elements spread through the universe?
flashcards.back: By the explosion of massive stars (supernovae).
A remnant with gravity so strong that not even light can escape.
A white dwarf that has cooled and no longer emits significant energy.

flashcards.front: Which elements can be made by fusion in red giants and super giants?
flashcards.back: Helium and heavier elements, up to iron.

questions.question: What is the first stage in the life cycle of every star?
markScheme: 1 mark: Nebula
questions.explanation: All stars start as a nebula, a cloud of dust and gas, which then forms a protostar.

questions.question: What will a star about the same size as the Sun become after the main sequence?
markScheme: 1 mark: A red giant
questions.explanation: Sun-sized stars become red giants. Red super giants come from much more massive stars.

questions.question: What is the final stage of a star about the same size as the Sun?
markScheme: 1 mark: Black dwarf
questions.explanation: A white dwarf cools and fades to become a black dwarf.

questions.question: What is the explosion of a massive star called?
markScheme: 1 mark: A supernova
questions.explanation: A red super giant ends its life in a supernova explosion.

questions.question: What decides whether a star becomes a red giant or a red super giant?
markScheme: 1 mark: Its size (mass)
questions.explanation: The life cycle after the main sequence depends on the star's size (mass).

questions.question: What can be left after a supernova?
options: A neutron star or a black hole
A white dwarf or a black dwarf
A protostar or a nebula only
markScheme: 1 mark: A neutron star or a black hole
questions.explanation: The core of a supernova becomes a neutron star, or a black hole for the most massive stars.

questions.question: Which process produces helium in a main sequence star?
markScheme: 1 mark: Fusion of hydrogen nuclei
questions.explanation: Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium nuclei, releasing energy.

questions.question: Where are elements heavier than iron produced?
markScheme: 1 mark: In supernovae
questions.explanation: Fusion in stars only makes elements up to iron; heavier elements are produced in the extreme conditions of a supernova.

questions.question: The Earth contains gold. What does this tell us about the material that formed the solar system?
options: It came only from the Big Bang
It was made in the Sun's core
It included material from at least one earlier supernova
It came from a white dwarf
markScheme: 1 mark: It included material from at least one earlier supernova
questions.explanation: Gold is heavier than iron, so it can only have been made in a supernova. The solar system formed from a nebula that contained this material.

questions.question: Which sequence is correct for a star much more massive than the Sun?
options: Nebula, protostar, main sequence, red super giant, supernova, neutron star
Nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf
Protostar, nebula, main sequence, red super giant, black dwarf
Nebula, main sequence, protostar, supernova, red super giant, black hole
markScheme: 1 mark: Nebula, protostar, main sequence, red super giant, supernova, neutron star
questions.explanation: Massive stars follow nebula, protostar, main sequence, red super giant, supernova, then neutron star or black hole.

questions.question: Name the stage that comes immediately after a protostar.
markScheme: 1 mark: main sequence star
questions.explanation: When fusion starts, the protostar becomes a main sequence star.

questions.question: Name the two possible final stages of a star much more massive than the Sun.
markScheme: 1 mark: neutron star
1 mark: black hole
questions.explanation: The remnant after a supernova depends on how massive the core is.

questions.question: Describe what a nebula is and what force acts to form a star from it.
markScheme: 1 mark: a cloud of dust and gas
1 mark: gravity (gravitational attraction) pulls it together
questions.explanation: Gravity is the starting point of every star's life.

questions.question: Explain why a main sequence star is stable.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravity pulls inwards; fusion energy causes an outward pressure (expansion)
1 mark: these are balanced (in equilibrium)
questions.explanation: Balanced forces mean the star stays the same size.

questions.question: Describe what happens to a star like the Sun after it has been a red giant.
markScheme: 1 mark: it becomes a white dwarf (outer layers drift away, core collapses)
1 mark: the white dwarf cools to become a black dwarf
questions.explanation: The final stages are white dwarf then black dwarf.

questions.question: Explain how elements are distributed throughout the universe.
markScheme: 1 mark: massive stars explode as supernovae
1 mark: the explosion throws the elements made in the star out into space
questions.explanation: This material later forms new nebulae, stars and planets.

questions.question: Explain how fusion processes lead to the formation of new elements in stars.
markScheme: 1 mark: in main sequence stars, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium
1 mark: in red giants and red super giants, helium and heavier nuclei fuse to form elements up to iron
1 mark: elements heavier than iron are formed in a supernova
questions.explanation: Successive fusion stages build up heavier nuclei; only the energy of a supernova can make elements beyond iron.

questions.question: Suggest why a star stays on the main sequence for much longer than it stays a red giant.
markScheme: 1 mark: the star contains a very large amount of hydrogen to fuse during the main sequence
1 mark: once core hydrogen runs low, later stages use fuel faster or have less fuel, so they are much shorter
questions.explanation: Hydrogen fusion is the longest, most stable stage of a star's life.

questions.question: Name the element that is mainly fused in main sequence stars.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen
questions.explanation: Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium.

questions.question: Compare a white dwarf with a black dwarf.
markScheme: 1 mark: a white dwarf is very hot and dense and gives out a lot of light
1 mark: a black dwarf is a white dwarf that has cooled and no longer emits significant energy
questions.explanation: A black dwarf is simply the cooled final state of a white dwarf.

questions.question: Describe the life cycle of a star about the same size as the Sun.
markScheme: Indicative content: nebula (cloud of dust and gas); gravity pulls it together to form a protostar; it gets hotter and denser until fusion of hydrogen to helium starts; main sequence star: stable as gravity balances outward pressure from fusion; when hydrogen runs low, expands to a red giant; helium fuses to heavier elements; outer layers drift away; core becomes a white dwarf; white dwarf cools to a black dwarf.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): all stages in the correct order with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some stages named, possibly with errors in order.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Six stages: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf.

questions.question: Compare the life cycles of a star the size of the Sun and a star much more massive than the Sun. Include how each produces new elements.
markScheme: Indicative content: both start as a nebula pulled together by gravity, become a protostar, then a main sequence star fusing hydrogen into helium, stable because gravity balances fusion pressure; Sun-sized: red giant, fuses helium to heavier elements such as carbon; outer layers drift away; white dwarf; cools to black dwarf; massive: red super giant; fuses heavier nuclei up to iron; core collapses, supernova explosion; elements heavier than iron produced in the supernova; elements distributed through the universe; remnant is a neutron star or black hole (most massive); the path depends on the mass of the star.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear comparison of both cycles in the correct order with correct links to element formation, including elements heavier than iron in supernovae.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both cycles mostly correct with some reference to element formation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one cycle partly described or simple statements.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Same start, different ends. Only massive stars make elements heavier than iron, in supernovae.

questions.question: What is a black hole?
options: An object whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape
markScheme: 1 mark: An object whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape
questions.explanation: A black hole forms from the most massive stars after a supernova. A cooled white dwarf is a black dwarf.

questions.question: A star has a mass about 20 times that of the Sun. Which pair of stages will it pass through, in this order, after the main sequence?
markScheme: 1 mark: Red super giant, then supernova
questions.explanation: A star much more massive than the Sun becomes a red super giant and then explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole. Red giant and white dwarf are stages for Sun-sized stars.

questions.question: Explain why a protostar gets hotter as it forms.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravity pulls the dust and gas inwards, so it becomes denser
1 mark: the particles speed up and collide more, so the temperature increases
questions.explanation: Gravitational collapse heats the protostar until fusion can begin.

questions.question: Explain why scientists say that we are made of 'star dust'.
markScheme: Indicative content: elements in our bodies such as carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and iron were made by fusion in stars; heavier elements made in supernovae; supernovae spread elements into space; this material formed new nebulae; the solar system, Earth and living things formed from this material.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): links fusion in stars, supernova distribution and formation of the solar system.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example elements come from stars.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Elements made in earlier stars were scattered by supernovae and gathered into the nebula that formed the Sun and Earth.
